raw_evidence.label: Origin: The Economist's 'TV's golden age is real' (24 Nov 2018)
raw_evidence.content: This dataset was assembled by The Economist's Graphic Detail team for an article titled 'TV's golden age is real,' published on 24 November 2018. The piece used IMDb user ratings for every American TV drama series available on IMDb from 1990 to 2018 to ask whether the cultural intuition about a 'Golden Age of TV' is supported by audience scoring. The published chart was a scatter of season-by-season average IMDb ratings against premiere date, with the premise that if quality has truly risen since the late 1990s the dot cloud should drift upward over time. The CSV provided is exactly the data that drove that scatter plot. Each row is one season of one drama, with seven fields: titleId (IMDb tt-id), seasonNumber, title, the season's premiere date, av_rating (the season's average rating on IMDb), share (what fraction of total votes that season received), and a comma-separated genre tag. The data file ships with a README that names IMDb, OMDb (for region/airing dates), and The Economist's own scripting as the three sources.

raw_evidence.label: What 'Golden Age' means in TV criticism (1999 → ~2023)
raw_evidence.content: When critics talk about a contemporary 'Golden Age' of television they mean a roughly 25-year stretch beginning with HBO's The Sopranos in January 1999 and running through the prestige-drama explosion of the 2000s and 2010s. Wikipedia's reference article dates the period 2000–2023; The Sopranos is the canonical opening shot. The era is defined by cinematic production budgets, serialized rather than episodic storytelling, and morally ambiguous anti-hero leads — Tony Soprano, Don Draper, Walter White, Stringer Bell. Production values on shows like Mad Men, Breaking Bad, and Band of Brothers came to rival theatrical film, and HBO's blueprint was copied first by AMC (Mad Men 2007, Breaking Bad 2008) and then aggressively by Netflix (House of Cards 2013) and the rest of the streamers. Crucially for this dataset, almost the entire 'Golden Age' falls inside the 1990–2018 window the IMDb data covers — so if it really happened, it should be visible in the ratings.

Wikipedia's reference article dates the period 2000–2023; The Sopranos is the canonical opening shot. The era is defined by cinematic production budgets, serialized rather than episodic storytelling, and morally ambiguous anti-hero leads — Tony Soprano, Don Draper, Walter White, Stringer Bell. Production values on shows like Mad Men, Breaking Bad, and Band of Brothers came to rival theatrical film, and HBO's blueprint was copied first by AMC (Mad Men 2007, Breaking Bad 2008) and then aggressively by Netflix (House of Cards 2013) and the rest of the streamers. Crucially for this dataset, almost the entire 'Golden Age' falls inside the 1990–2018 window the IMDb data covers — so if it really happened, it should be visible in the ratings.

raw_evidence.label: Origin: The Economist's 'TV's golden age is real' (24 Nov 2018)
raw_evidence.content: This dataset was assembled by The Economist's Graphic Detail team for an article titled 'TV's golden age is real,' published on 24 November 2018. The piece used IMDb user ratings for every American TV drama series available on IMDb from 1990 to 2018 to ask whether the cultural intuition about a 'Golden Age of TV' is supported by audience scoring. The published chart was a scatter of season-by-season average IMDb ratings against premiere date, with the premise that if quality has truly risen since the late 1990s the dot cloud should drift upward over time. The CSV provided is exactly the data that drove that scatter plot. Each row is one season of one drama, with seven fields: titleId (IMDb tt-id), seasonNumber, title, the season's premiere date, av_rating (the season's average rating on IMDb), share (what fraction of total votes that season received), and a comma-separated genre tag. The data file ships with a README that names IMDb, OMDb (for region/airing dates), and The Economist's own scripting as the three sources.

The visible step changes are 1990s≈7.88, early-2000s≈8.0, 2014-2018≈8.15-8.28. The single highest median year is 2014 at 8.28, which lines up with peak Breaking Bad / Game of Thrones / True Detective territory. The lowest median year is 1992 at 7.82, on a thin sample of just 10 seasons. Translation: the 'Golden Age' is real in the data, but as a quarter-point lift in the *typical* show, not a wholesale revolution.

raw_evidence.label: The floor rises, the ceiling does not — and that is the real Golden Age signal
raw_evidence.content: Splitting each year's seasons into floor (10th percentile), median (50th), and ceiling (90th) reveals the most counterintuitive finding: the so-called Golden Age is mostly a *floor* phenomenon. Comparing 1995 to 2017, the floor rises from 7.01 to 7.23 (+0.22), the median rises from 7.80 to 8.12 (+0.32) — but the ceiling is essentially flat, drifting from 8.96 to 8.90 (-0.06). The very best 1990s shows scored as well as the very best 2010s shows. What changed is that the bottom decile of mid-2010s drama is roughly a quarter-point better than the bottom decile of mid-1990s drama. Cable and streaming did not invent a new category of brilliance; they raised the standard for unremarkable.

sentences.summary: det_03: Peak TV: explosion of scripted series 2002 → 2018. Source: The End of Peak TV: 516 Original Scripted Series Aired in 2023 — Variety (https://variety.com/2024/tv/news/peak-tv-tally-original-scripted-series-aired-20) Facts: 182 original scripted series in 2002; 343 in 2013 Source: Peak TV Update — IndieWire 2018 (https://www.indiewire.com/2018/08/peak-tv-update-fx-john-landgraf-scripted-12019) Facts: Landgraf in 2018: 'the Golden Age of Television has become the Gilded Age of Television'; 319 scripted series counted in the first half of 2018, +5% YoY

raw_evidence.label: Peak TV: explosion of scripted series 2002 → 2018
raw_evidence.content: Parallel to the rise in quality is a separate but related story: the sheer *number* of original scripted series exploded. FX boss John Landgraf, who has tracked the count for two decades, recorded 182 scripted series in 2002, 343 by 2013, 487 by 2017, then 559 in 2021 and a peak of 600 in 2022. Within the dataset window (through 2018), the count roughly tripled. Landgraf's coinage 'Peak TV' captured the worry that quality could not keep pace with quantity — by 2018 he was already calling it a 'Gilded Age' rather than a Golden one. This matters for the data because the scatter must be denser at the right (more shows = more dots) without being meaningfully *higher* if Landgraf was right. If the dot cloud rises *and* gets denser, both the Golden Age and the Peak TV theses are supported.

raw_evidence.content: The number of American drama seasons released per year exploded. In 1990 the dataset records 22 seasons. By 2017 — the last full year — it records 230. That is a 10.5x increase. The growth is monotonic from 2002 onward (apart from a small 2008-writers'-strike dip): 42 in 2002, 90 in 2007, 142 in 2013, 215 in 2016. 2018 shows 184 seasons but only because the dataset cuts off in October. This matches FX boss John Landgraf's industry-wide tally — 182 scripted shows in 2002 and 487 by 2017 — so the dataset is tracking the same Peak TV phenomenon, not just a sampling artefact.

def pct(vals, p):
    s = sorted(vals)
    if not s:
        return None
    i = (len(s) - 1) * p
    lo, hi = int(i), min(int(i) + 1, len(s) - 1)
    frac = i - lo
    return s[lo] * (1 - frac) + s[hi] * frac

raw_evidence.label: What 'Golden Age' means in TV criticism (1999 → ~2023)
raw_evidence.content: When critics talk about a contemporary 'Golden Age' of television they mean a roughly 25-year stretch beginning with HBO's The Sopranos in January 1999 and running through the prestige-drama explosion of the 2000s and 2010s. Wikipedia's reference article dates the period 2000–2023; The Sopranos is the canonical opening shot. The era is defined by cinematic production budgets, serialized rather than episodic storytelling, and morally ambiguous anti-hero leads — Tony Soprano, Don Draper, Walter White, Stringer Bell. Production values on shows like Mad Men, Breaking Bad, and Band of Brothers came to rival theatrical film, and HBO's blueprint was copied first by AMC (Mad Men 2007, Breaking Bad 2008) and then aggressively by Netflix (House of Cards 2013) and the rest of the streamers. Crucially for this dataset, almost the entire 'Golden Age' falls inside the 1990–2018 window the IMDb data covers — so if it really happened, it should be visible in the ratings.

The Wire is unusually flat for a 'great' show at 8.24-8.42, slow-build television that IMDb voters never spiked. Breaking Bad is the cleanest growth curve in the data: 8.71 → 8.77 → 8.75 → 9.11 → 9.55 over five seasons. Mad Men climbs from 8.23 to 8.85 over seven seasons. Game of Thrones is the most volatile: a high opening (9.13), a peak in S6 (9.49), and a foreshadowing dip in S7 (9.30) before the dataset cuts off. None of these legendary shows started with their best season — every one of them rose, season over season, suggesting prestige-era audiences gave shows time to grow into themselves.

sentences.summary: det_04: IMDb rating bias: self-selection, fan-survivorship, recency. Source: The Problem With IMDb's Rating System — The Ringer (https://www.theringer.com/2019/06/12/tv/imdb-rating-system-problems-chernobyl) Facts: IMDb ratings are aggregated user votes from a self-selected, unverified pool; Voters who feel strongly (positive or negative) are over-represented Source: Why do user ratings often decrease over time? — IMDb Help (https://help.imdb.com/article/imdb/track-movies-tv/why-do-the-user-ratings-on-ma) Facts: Initial ratings are heavily skewed toward the high end because early voters are usually fans; Ratings drift down as casual viewers eventually weigh in Source: Game of Thrones lowest-rated episodes — Collider (https://collider.com/game-of-thrones-lowest-rated-episodes-imdb/) Facts: Game of Thrones series finale 'The Iron Throne' rated 4.0/10; Before season 8 no Game of Thrones episode had scored below 8.0/10

raw_evidence.label: IMDb rating bias: self-selection, fan-survivorship, recency
raw_evidence.content: Before treating IMDb scores as 'TV quality' it is worth knowing how those scores are made. IMDb ratings are aggregated 1–10 votes from a self-selected pool of registered users, which produces three structural biases: (1) self-selection — viewers who feel strongly are over-represented and middling opinions disappear; (2) fan survivorship — people who watch a season to the end and then rate it tend to be fans, which inflates television scores relative to films; (3) early-rating skew — the first wave of voters is the most enthusiastic, so brand-new seasons land higher and drift down later. Average drama ratings on IMDb cluster around 8 out of 10 — far above the theoretical midpoint of 5.5 — for exactly this reason. The infamous Game of Thrones final-season collapse (the series finale fell to 4.0/10, the lowest score in any of the show's eight seasons) is the same mechanism running in reverse: angry viewers self-select to vote down. None of this kills the dataset as a tool for spotting trends; it just means absolute levels say more about who shows up to vote than about objective quality, while differences between seasons and shows are still meaningful.

raw_evidence.label: IMDb rating bias: self-selection, fan-survivorship, recency
raw_evidence.content: Before treating IMDb scores as 'TV quality' it is worth knowing how those scores are made. IMDb ratings are aggregated 1–10 votes from a self-selected pool of registered users, which produces three structural biases: (1) self-selection — viewers who feel strongly are over-represented and middling opinions disappear; (2) fan survivorship — people who watch a season to the end and then rate it tend to be fans, which inflates television scores relative to films; (3) early-rating skew — the first wave of voters is the most enthusiastic, so brand-new seasons land higher and drift down later. Average drama ratings on IMDb cluster around 8 out of 10 — far above the theoretical midpoint of 5.5 — for exactly this reason. The infamous Game of Thrones final-season collapse (the series finale fell to 4.0/10, the lowest score in any of the show's eight seasons) is the same mechanism running in reverse: angry viewers self-select to vote down. None of this kills the dataset as a tool for spotting trends; it just means absolute levels say more about who shows up to vote than about objective quality, while differences between seasons and shows are still meaningful.

raw_evidence.label: IMDb rating bias: self-selection, fan-survivorship, recency
raw_evidence.content: Before treating IMDb scores as 'TV quality' it is worth knowing how those scores are made. IMDb ratings are aggregated 1–10 votes from a self-selected pool of registered users, which produces three structural biases: (1) self-selection — viewers who feel strongly are over-represented and middling opinions disappear; (2) fan survivorship — people who watch a season to the end and then rate it tend to be fans, which inflates television scores relative to films; (3) early-rating skew — the first wave of voters is the most enthusiastic, so brand-new seasons land higher and drift down later. Average drama ratings on IMDb cluster around 8 out of 10 — far above the theoretical midpoint of 5.5 — for exactly this reason. The infamous Game of Thrones final-season collapse (the series finale fell to 4.0/10, the lowest score in any of the show's eight seasons) is the same mechanism running in reverse: angry viewers self-select to vote down. None of this kills the dataset as a tool for spotting trends; it just means absolute levels say more about who shows up to vote than about objective quality, while differences between seasons and shows are still meaningful.

raw_evidence.label: What 'Golden Age' means in TV criticism (1999 → ~2023)
raw_evidence.content: When critics talk about a contemporary 'Golden Age' of television they mean a roughly 25-year stretch beginning with HBO's The Sopranos in January 1999 and running through the prestige-drama explosion of the 2000s and 2010s. Wikipedia's reference article dates the period 2000–2023; The Sopranos is the canonical opening shot. The era is defined by cinematic production budgets, serialized rather than episodic storytelling, and morally ambiguous anti-hero leads — Tony Soprano, Don Draper, Walter White, Stringer Bell. Production values on shows like Mad Men, Breaking Bad, and Band of Brothers came to rival theatrical film, and HBO's blueprint was copied first by AMC (Mad Men 2007, Breaking Bad 2008) and then aggressively by Netflix (House of Cards 2013) and the rest of the streamers. Crucially for this dataset, almost the entire 'Golden Age' falls inside the 1990–2018 window the IMDb data covers — so if it really happened, it should be visible in the ratings.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: TV is the dominant cultural form of the streaming era
raw_evidence.content: Asking whether TV drama is genuinely getting better is not a niche aesthetic question. By 2018, when this dataset was assembled, the average American household watched several hours of scripted television daily, streaming services were displacing theatrical film as the cultural centerpiece, and HBO/Netflix originals were displacing Hollywood films at the Emmys and in critic year-end lists. If the perceived 'Golden Age' is real — if quality really has risen — that is a story about how an entire art form re-organized itself around the long-form serialized drama in less than two decades. If it is illusory — if we have just been telling ourselves a flattering story while watching a few hits and ignoring the floor — that matters too, because policymakers, advertisers, and an entire cultural-criticism industry have built their narratives on the assumption that the Golden Age is settled fact.

raw_evidence.content: Asking whether TV drama is genuinely getting better is not a niche aesthetic question. This top ten is the strongest evidence against a 'rising ceiling' story — the very top of the distribution looks era-blind.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: rising floor vs. rising ceiling
raw_evidence.content: There is a subtle distinction worth holding on to before looking at the numbers. A 'Golden Age' could mean two very different things in the data: either the *ceiling* has risen (the very best shows in 2015 are better than the very best shows in 1995) or the *floor* has risen (mediocre 2015 dramas are better than mediocre 1995 dramas, while the top stays similar). Most cultural critics talk as though both are true. But IMDb's structural ceiling sits around 9.5 — Breaking Bad's final seasons, Band of Brothers, Chernobyl all bunch up there. So if there is room to move it is mainly the *floor* that can rise. Watch for that distinction: a clear upward drift in the *median* season rating is stronger evidence than an upward drift in the *maximum*, because the max is capped by IMDb's voting culture itself.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: TV is the dominant cultural form of the streaming era
raw_evidence.content: Asking whether TV drama is genuinely getting better is not a niche aesthetic question. By 2018, when this dataset was assembled, the average American household watched several hours of scripted television daily, streaming services were displacing theatrical film as the cultural centerpiece, and HBO/Netflix originals were displacing Hollywood films at the Emmys and in critic year-end lists. If the perceived 'Golden Age' is real — if quality really has risen — that is a story about how an entire art form re-organized itself around the long-form serialized drama in less than two decades. If it is illusory — if we have just been telling ourselves a flattering story while watching a few hits and ignoring the floor — that matters too, because policymakers, advertisers, and an entire cultural-criticism industry have built their narratives on the assumption that the Golden Age is settled fact.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: rising floor vs. rising ceiling
raw_evidence.content: There is a subtle distinction worth holding on to before looking at the numbers. A 'Golden Age' could mean two very different things in the data: either the *ceiling* has risen (the very best shows in 2015 are better than the very best shows in 1995) or the *floor* has risen (mediocre 2015 dramas are better than mediocre 1995 dramas, while the top stays similar). Most cultural critics talk as though both are true. But IMDb's structural ceiling sits around 9.5 — Breaking Bad's final seasons, Band of Brothers, Chernobyl all bunch up there. So if there is room to move it is mainly the *floor* that can rise. Watch for that distinction: a clear upward drift in the *median* season rating is stronger evidence than an upward drift in the *maximum*, because the max is capped by IMDb's voting culture itself.
